consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Oh, I'm so worried about his eyesight. He sits way too close to the TV when watching cartoons and also when reading books. I've tried to get him to move back a bit, but he says he can't see as well then.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Sometimes I call his name and he doesn't respond right away. It's like he's not hearing me or maybe just ignoring me? But if I go over to him and say it again، he'll usually answer. I don't know if it's his hearing or just him being a bit distracted.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: His teeth are a worry for me because the dentist said the enamel is weak. We have to be super careful with sugary foods and make sure he brushes them really well to prevent cavities.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: When he plays outside with friends， his breathing gets much faster than the other kids. Even when they're all running around together， my son seems to be panting more. I've mentioned it to his dad， but we haven't done anything about it yet.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Poor baby... he has low muscle tone. The physiotherapist is working with him to improve it. You can see it when he walks or tries to hold things; it's just a bit more effortful for him than for other kids his age.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Eating can be tricky sometimes. He's super fussy about food textures and won't eat certain things because of how they feel in his mouth. Like， mashed potatoes are okay but not if they're lumpy at all.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Yes... his fingers are shorter than usual. We were told it's just something he was born with and doesn't affect anything else.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences faster breathing when playing outside with friends, suggesting potential cardiac concerns.

Additionally, tethered cord, delayed closure of the soft spot on the head, undescended testes, skeletal anomalies, and palatal abnormalities may be present in some individuals with KBG syndrome. a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires regular heart check-ups to monitor a potential heart condition.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a feeding aversion, making mealtime challenging and leading to difficulties in getting a balanced diet.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delays, is less coordinated when moving, and speaks less than expected at her age, which concerns her parents about her language development and potential impact on her education.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may have speech delay which may be linked to their seizure experiences.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has experienced otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss, and her hearing is somewhat selective.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many children with KBG syndrome have had otitis media or glue ear, which can lead to conductive hearing loss and affect their hearing abilities.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has astigmatism, which affects her vision and makes it difficult for her to focus on distant objects.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness, which can impact their daily life and learning.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has weak enamel and requires regular dental care to prevent cavities.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding aversion and difficulty eating balanced diets can be challenges for those with KBG syndrome.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient's speech delay and developmental delays have impacted her academic performance and communication skills.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and some may require EHCP support, but there are varying levels of educational attainment, with some children staying in mainstream education and obtaining qualifications.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delays, is less coordinated when moving, and speaks less than expected at her age, which concerns her parents about her language development and potential impact on her education.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome may experience behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety, and some may have speech delay which may be linked to their corresponding conditions.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, which can cause scoliosis, and there have been concerns about asymmetric hip creases and an asymmetric or painful gait.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Some individuals with KBG syndrome have had tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, and sacral dimple, among other complications.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires regular heart check-ups to monitor a potential heart condition, and has weak enamel on her teeth, necessitating regular dental care.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Honestly, I'm worried about his eyesight. He complains that things look blurry sometimes, and it's hard to know if it's just a phase or something more serious. I've noticed he squints or rubs his eyes frequently.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Yes... he seems to have trouble hearing certain sounds. Like, when we're watching TV, he'll ask us to turn it up because he can't hear it well. It's concerning because he should be able to pick up on conversations and shows easily at his age.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Chewing has become a challenge for him lately. Harder foods like apples or meat are difficult for him to manage. We've had to adjust his diet somewhat to softer foods to make mealtime less stressful.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Physical activity... he just can't seem to keep up with the other kids. Even simple games like tag or running around leave him winded and tired quickly. It worries me that there might be an underlying issue we need to address.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: The tethered cord issue is something we're closely monitoring. The specialists have assured us they're on top of it, but it's still a concern for us as parents.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Mealtime... it's often a struggle. He has days where eating is just really hard for him. The food either doesn't agree with him or he's just not interested. We try to keep a routine and offer a variety of foods to see what works best for him.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Well... aside from what we've discussed, his movements are slightly different from his peers. And he was diagnosed with scoliosis. These are things we're working through with his therapists and doctors to ensure he gets the right support and care.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a valve issue in her heart that requires regular check-ups every few months.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient is very picky with food textures and has trouble eating certain foods due to texture aversions.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences falls more often than other kids her age, and she has speech delay with slow progress despite therapy.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may have developmental delay and behavioral differences.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has otitis media and glue ear, requiring frequent medical attention.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many children with KBG syndrome have experienced otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has myopia and hypermetropia, affecting her vision.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has weak enamel and requires regular dental care to prevent tooth damage.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and lack of interest in feeding can be significant and long-lasting in some individuals with KBG syndrome.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has speech delay and takes longer to catch up with her peers in terms of academic performance.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, though some go to a mainstream primary school and others may require more support and may need to attend specialized settings.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences speech delay and falls more often, which can lead to fears and anxieties.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome may have developmental delay and behavioral differences, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, which can cause scoliosis, and delayed closure of the soft spot on her head.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Some individuals with KBG syndrome have an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and delayed closure of the soft spot on the head (anterior fontanelle).

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs regular heart check-ups, has weak enamel, experiences speech delay, and falls more often.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes; approximately 20-40% have seizures; and many have developmental delay and behavioral differences.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a pre-existing heart condition that requires regular check-ups, and the doctors keep a close eye on his heart.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient is slower to gain weight compared to his peers, and his eating habits are monitored closely to ensure he gets enough nutrients.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences moments where he stares off into space for a few seconds, which can be unsettling due to the lack of responsiveness during these episodes.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and medication(s) may be appropriate in some circumstances.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has experienced otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss and affect his hearing.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many children with KBG syndrome have had fluid in the ear, which can lead to conductive hearing loss.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has myopia, which means he has trouble seeing things that are far away.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient's teeth are weak and prone to breaking or chipping, requiring regular dental check-ups and careful brushing.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and tooth sensitivity are common in individuals with KBG syndrome.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty gaining weight and requires close monitoring of eating habits.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, though some go to a mainstream primary school and others may need more support and may require EHCP.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences moments of staring off into space for brief periods, which can be concerning.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome often have behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of his spinal bones, which can cause scoliosis.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: A proportion of individuals with KBG syndrome have subtler anomalies of the roof of the mouth (palate), which can affect speech development and feeding.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs regular heart check-ups, and there are concerns about hormonal imbalances and palatal abnormalities.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Approximately 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Additionally, 11% have tethered cord, and some children may experience delays in closing of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle).

== CLINICAL REFERENCE GUIDELINES ==

What is KBG syndrome?
KBG syndrome was first described in 1975, and its name is derived from the initials of the first three patients reported with the condition. People with KBG syndrome have a characteristic (and sometimes subtle) facial appearance, very large permanent teeth, and variable degrees of developmental delay, learning difficulties and behavioural differences. Because the facial features can be subtle and are not always present, the diagnosis may not be made until the permanent teeth have come through. Other features seen in some affected individuals include conductive hearing loss, undescended testes in boys, seizures, skeletal anomalies and short stature. KBG syndrome is caused by changes (variants) in, or a deletion of, the ANKRD11 gene in chromosome 16 (band q24.3). Most affected people are the first person in their family to carry the gene change, but a small proportion have inherited it from a parent, who is likely to have features of KBG syndrome. The condition affects boys and girls, and there are both mildly and more significantly affected individuals of both sexes. However, there appear to be some reports of more affected males than females but the reason for this is unclear.
Most people with KBG syndrome have:
A degree of developmental delay and some element of behavioural differences. Large permanent upper teeth (macrodontia of upper central incisors). Characteristic facial appearance: a triangular-shaped face; wide-spaced eyes and thick eyebrows, which sometimes join in the centre (synophrys). Short fingers (brachydactyly) with curved 5th finger (clinodactyly)
How common is KBG syndrome?
KBG Syndrome is rare and thought to affect several hundred people worldwide. It is likely that many people are not diagnosed because many of the features can be mild in those with a change (variant) in ANKRD11, including the degree of learning (intellectual) disability. KBG Syndrome is one of the most prevalent causes of syndromic developmental delay. This guide is designed to help families and healthcare professionals looking after people affected by KBG syndrome. It contains information about the cause, the ways in which it can affect people and suggestions about the help and management that can benefit people with this condition. What causes KBG syndrome?
KBG syndrome is caused by one copy of the ANKRD11 gene not functioning properly. This may be due to a change within the gene that disrupts its function, or to the loss (deletion) of the whole gene or part of it. The other copy is unaffected. Why did this happen?
When children are conceived, their parents’ genetic material (DNA) is copied in the egg and sperm that makes a new child. The biological copying method is not perfect and occasionally random, rare changes occur in the genetic code of children that are not seen in the DNA of their parents. KBG syndrome occurs when one of these random, rare changes affects the ANKRD11 gene in chromosome 16. This happens naturally and is not due to the biological parents’ diet, environment or lifestyle. In most people with KBG syndrome, the genetic change was a random (or “de novo”) change, meaning the change occurred for the first time in that family in the affected individual. Occasionaly, one parent may have the same change (variant) and pass it on to their child. No one should be blamed for variants in their DNA and no parent is at fault when a new DNA change occurs in their child. Can it happen again?
The possibility of having another child affected by a rare gene disorder depends on the genetic code of the parents. In most families, the genetic change has happened for the first time in the child with KBG syndrome. We call this a ‘de novo’ change. In this situation, when parents are unaffected, the chances of having another child with the same condition are very low (usually less than 1%). One reason why there is some residual chance of recurrence is due to a rare phenomenon called germline mosaicism. This is when a parent carries a genetic change, but it is limited to some of their egg or sperm cells. The genetic change would not, therefore, be detected in the parents’ blood tests. Unique publishes a short general guide to mosaicism that covers this phenomenon. If a parent has KBG syndrome, the chances of passing the condition on to a child are much higher at 50%, or 1 chance in 2, as the parent could either pass on their altered copy of the gene or the unaffected copy. This inheritance pattern is called autosomal dominant (because the change is on an autosomal chromosome and an outcome can be seen if only one copy of the gene is altered). Unique publishes a separate guide to single gene disorders -autosomal dominant inheritance. Each family situation is different, and a clinical geneticist or genetic counsellor can give specific advice for your family. Development:
Developmental delay has been reported in almost all children with KBG syndrome. The degree of delay ranges from mild (in most) to severe (in few). Developmental “milestones”, including rolling, sitting, walking, playing with toys, using cutlery, using zips and buttons, and toilet training, are often delayed, although there is a wide range of eventual ability, with some children acquiring mobility and other skills around the same age as “typical” children and others showing more obvious delay. Learning:
Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, though some go to a mainstream primary school. The extra demands of mainstream secondary school may prove too challenging, and children may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP). b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences bowel movements issues, including accidents and trouble with regularity.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and constipation or diarrhea can be common in individuals with KBG syndrome.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has epilepsy, requiring careful management and regular medication.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which may require medication or surgery.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has experienced otitis media or glue ear, leading to discomfort and difficulty hearing.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many individuals with KBG syndrome have had otitis media or glue ear, affecting their hearing and comfort.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has astigmatism, which affects her vision and clarity of sight.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and myopia or hypermetropia.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty chewing harder foods and requires regular dental check-ups.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Dental concerns such as weak enamel and need for frequent dental procedures are common in individuals with KBG syndrome.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty keeping up with physical activity and needs additional support in school.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and some may require special schooling or support from EHCP.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty keeping up with physical activity and developmentally delays compared to peers.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome typically develop slightly slower than typical, with some showing significant delays in reaching developmental milestones.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, which may lead to complications such as scoliosis.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: A study found that 11% of children with KBG syndrome have tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait.

   - Cardiac review (including echo and ECG)

   - Address heart conditions with surgery or monitoring
   - Manage tethered cord with MRI
   - Monitor growth velocity if height is below the 2nd centile

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences heart rate increases when engaging in physical activities, requiring ongoing monitoring but not causing significant concern at this time.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes, with some needing surgery or monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty eating certain foods and often feels full quickly, making meal times stressful.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences seizures, which are managed with a plan.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which typically respond to anti-epileptic treatments.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has experienced otitis media or glue ear, which has led to conductive hearing loss and requires periodic hearing checks.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many individuals with KBG syndrome have had otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss and require treatment.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has hypermetropia, requiring glasses for clearer vision.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long sightedness.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires frequent dental visits due to cavities and weak enamel.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Feeding difficulties and tooth decay are common in individuals with KBG syndrome, requiring regular dental care and monitoring.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient enters puberty within the typical age range but shows developmental delays compared to peers.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and some may require Education Health Care Plans (EHCP).

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient is generally behind other kids her age in terms of overall development.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Developmental delay is a common feature in KBG syndrome, with a wide range of abilities among affected individuals.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of his spinal bones, which can lead to scoliosis.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Individuals with KBG syndrome may have an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and some have tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Recommendations for screening:
   - Regular dental check-ups
   - Regular hearing reviews (age 5)
   - Ophthalmology review
   - Palatal review (if concerns arise)

b) Recommendations for treatments:
   - Manage seizures with medication
   - Monitor heart condition (ongoing monitoring and potential surgery)
   - Address tethered cord with MRI if concerns arise
   - Monitor development and provide additional support where needed
